scenes.tts: How can the Bay's crab estimate jump when the Bay has not grown? Watch a survey boat cross the winter water. Its dredge catches some crabs buried in the mud. Those catches become an estimate for the whole Bay. A moving estimate does not require a moving shoreline.
scenes.caption: How can the Bay's crab estimate jump when the Bay has not grown? Watch a survey boat cross the winter water. Its dredge catches some crabs buried in the mud. Those catches become an estimate for the whole Bay. A moving estimate does not require a moving shoreline.
scenes.visual: Fill the frame with a side view of Chesapeake Bay in winter. A GREY boat and dredge move left to right above BLUE schematic crab dots. Sample-site rings spread across a Bay outline, then transform into the label 'Bay-wide estimate'. Keep water drifting and the tow line moving.
scenes.narration: How can the Bay's crab estimate jump when the Bay has not grown? Watch a survey boat cross the winter water. Its dredge catches some crabs buried in the mud. Those catches become an estimate for the whole Bay. A moving estimate does not require a moving shoreline.

scenes.visual: Brief title card: 'Four Ways a Population Changes'. The Bay outline remains faintly behind the title and water continues moving.

scenes.tts: The earlier estimate appears as a bar. The next estimate appears beside it, much taller. These are estimates, not exact counts. The survey pattern is real, but it does not tell us the cause. So read height before hunting for explanations.

scenes.visual: Transform the Bay outline into computed bars labelled '367 million' and '852 million', with winters beneath them. Draw a dashed height at '734 million = twice 367'. Add 'estimates' above both bars. Bar heights must use the stated values.

scenes.tts: To explain the change, begin with a population. A population is every member of the same species living in the same place. Put the Bay's crabs inside one window. Now track what enters and leaves that window. The boundary matters because movement crosses it.
scenes.caption: To explain the change, begin with a population. A population is every member of the same species living in the same place. Put the Bay's crabs inside one window. Now track what enters and leaves that window. The boundary matters because movement crosses it.
scenes.visual: Bars fold into a large Bay-shaped window labelled 'blue crab population'. BLUE schematic crab dots drift inside. The window fills most of the frame. Its boundary pulses once as the words 'same species, same place' settle above it.
scenes.narration: To explain the change, begin with a population. A population is every member of the same species living in the same place. Put the Bay's crabs inside one window. Now track what enters and leaves that window. The boundary matters because movement crosses it.

scenes.tts: Births add crabs inside the window. Arrivals add crabs moving in. Deaths remove crabs. Departures remove crabs moving out. Call births and arrivals additions. Call deaths and departures losses. Population change is the balance between them. Additions and losses can occur at the same time while the population changes.
scenes.caption: Births add crabs inside the window. Arrivals add crabs moving in. Deaths remove crabs. Departures remove crabs moving out. Call births and arrivals additions. Call deaths and departures losses. Population change is the balance between them. Additions and losses can occur at the same time while the population changes.
scenes.visual: Carry the same Bay window. BLUE arrows labelled 'births' and 'arrivals' enter from the left as dots appear. RED arrows labelled 'deaths' and 'departures' leave on the right as dots fade or cross the boundary. Merge the left labels into 'additions' and right labels into 'losses'.
scenes.narration: Births add crabs inside the window. Arrivals add crabs moving in. Deaths remove crabs. Departures remove crabs moving out. Call births and arrivals additions. Call deaths and departures losses. Population change is the balance between them. Additions and losses can occur at the same time while the population changes.

scenes.tts: Imagine the loss arrows getting wider while the addition arrows stay unchanged. What should happen to the number of crabs inside? Follow the arrows before you decide. Watch the balance, not any single dot.
scenes.caption: Imagine the loss arrows getting wider while the addition arrows stay unchanged. What should happen to the number of crabs inside? Follow the arrows before you decide. Watch the balance, not any single dot.
scenes.visual: Keep the Bay window and both arrow groups. Slowly widen the RED loss arrows while BLUE addition arrows hold steady. Show the question 'Which way will the population move?' Do not reveal an answer. Label the dot count 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Imagine the loss arrows getting wider while the addition arrows stay unchanged. What should happen to the number of crabs inside? Follow the arrows before you decide. Watch the balance, not any single dot.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question. RED arrows continue a slow pulse, BLUE arrows drift steadily, and crab dots gently bob. Reveal nothing during the pause.

scenes.tts: The number falls because losses now exceed additions. Reverse the balance, and the number rises. Match the arrows, and the number stays steady. This gives the rule: populations rise when additions exceed losses, and fall when losses exceed additions. The dots show direction, not a forecast.

scenes.visual: First let RED arrows dominate and remove schematic dots. Then reset, let BLUE dominate, and add dots. Finally match arrow widths and hold the dot count. Under the carried window, write the guiding rule exactly as narrated.

scenes.tts: A limiting factor changes at least one addition or loss. A very cold winter can increase deaths. Better shelter can lower deaths among young crabs. Heavy harvest increases losses caused by people. Each factor matters through the same balance. Different factors can push the same arrow.
scenes.caption: A limiting factor changes at least one addition or loss. A very cold winter can increase deaths. Better shelter can lower deaths among young crabs. Heavy harvest increases losses caused by people. Each factor matters through the same balance. Different factors can push the same arrow.
scenes.visual: Keep the Bay window. A TEAL cold front thickens the RED deaths arrow. Reset. GREEN grass expands and narrows that arrow beside young crabs. Reset. A YELLOW crab pot feeds into the RED loss arrow. Mark every response 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: A limiting factor changes at least one addition or loss. A very cold winter can increase deaths. Better shelter can lower deaths among young crabs. Heavy harvest increases losses caused by people. Each factor matters through the same balance. Different factors can push the same arrow.

scenes.tts: The balance tells whether a population rises or falls over a chosen time. It cannot identify a cause by itself. Scientists need measurements of cold, shelter, predators, harvest, and other factors. The survey gives the pattern. Evidence about the arrows tests explanations. That extra evidence separates a pattern from a tested cause.

scenes.tts: Return to the winter bars. If the estimates are close to the truth, their jump means additions beat losses during the interval. The bars alone cannot say why. Keep the Bay window in mind. Every explanation must show which addition or loss changed, and what evidence supports it.
